deep.reconstruction:
This page is a working sheet for a reduction apparatus: annual aberration plus a lunar-node argument for nutation. It is dated 1818–1819 and set up for Göttingen in sidereal time. It continues the previous page, which derives the lunar node from Burckhardt's tables, and the next page, which gives instructions for entering a table with d+t+E+x.

(A) Annual aberration in right ascension and declination.
Notation: μ = aberration constant, ε = obliquity, Θ = Sun's longitude, α, δ = the star's RA and Dec.
Gauss defines three quantities:
- a = −μ sinε cosΘ
- b = −μ cosε cosΘ = M sinψ
- c = −μ sinΘ = M cosψ
Here M and ψ are an auxiliary modulus and angle, so that M² = b² + c² and tanψ = b/c (the M, ψ relations are my addition).
The page then states:
- Δα = (M/cosδ)·sin(ψ+α) = (cosα·b + sinα·c)/cosδ
- Δδ = a·cosδ + M·sinδ·cos(ψ+α) = cosδ·a − sinδ·sinα·b + sinδ·cosα·c
The expansions follow from:
- sin(ψ+α) = sinψ cosα + cosψ sinα
- cos(ψ+α) = cosψ cosα − sinψ sinα
These agree with the classical expressions:
- Δα·cosδ = −μ(cosε cosΘ cosα + sinΘ sinα)
- Δδ = −μ[cosε cosΘ(tanε cosδ − sinα sinδ) + sinΘ cosα sinδ]
This is exactly the later Bessel day-number form C = b, D = c, with a = C·tanε.

Constants (log10):
- log μ sinε = 0.91416
- log μ cosε = 1.27660
- log μ = 1.31408, i.e. μ ≈ 20.61″
- log tanε = 0.91416 − 1.27660 = 9.63756 − 10, hence a = b·tanε
The implied obliquity is ε ≈ 23°28′.

(B) Lunar node after Burckhardt, one value per year, 1818–1830.
The longitudes run from 45°7′31.7″ (1818) down to 173°1′50.3″ (1830). Successive differences alternate between 19°20′28.4″ and 19°20′28.5″. The 12-year total is 232°5′41.4″, a mean of 19°20′28.45″ per year.
This equals the daily motion 190.11586337″ multiplied by 366.2422 sidereal days. The previous page's 19°20′28.641″ per solar year is about 0.19″ larger (see errors).

(C) 'Columne': definitions of three table columns.
- (1) = (d + 1 2/9)·27.304333. Since 27.304333 = 10000/366.2422, this turns a day count d (offset by 11/9 day) into ten-thousandths of a year of 366.2422 sidereal days. This is my interpretation.
- (2) = 1 − 198.72·sin2☉, with the log written as 2.29894.
- (3) = −0.434·cos2☉, with log 0.434 = 9.63749 (correct).
Columns (2) and (3) are semi-annual solar terms; their physical meaning (nutation or another solar-period correction) is not certain from this page.

(D) Node argument in sidereal days.
- At 1819 Jan 1, 0h sidereal time Göttingen, the argument of the node is −487.74976 days.
- The daily motion is +190.11586337″ per sidereal day.
- The full period is 6816.89564 sidereal days; indeed 1296000″/190.11586337″ = 6816.89564.
The sign and size match the argument being the time since the node passed the equinox (Ω = 0). Burckhardt's 1819 node, 25°47′3.3″ = 92823.3″, minus about 94″ (about half a day of motion to the epoch), divided by 190.116″, gives ≈ 487.75. This is my check; the exact epoch offset is not stated.

Auxiliary multiples (mine: each is n × 190.11586337″):
- 500 d → 95057.931685″ = 26°24′17.931685″
- 400 d → 76046.345348″ = 21°7′26.345348″
- 300 d → 57034.759011″ = 15°50′34.759011″
- an interlined 10°33′43.172674″, which is the 200-day value (38023.172674″)

(E) Conversion to the table argument.
In the table the node-passage time has argument 3410, so table argument = 3410 + (days since Ω = 0).
- For 1819 Jan 0, 0h sidereal time: 3410 − 487.74976 − 1 = 2921.25024.
- Monthly entries add calendar days: Dec 0 1818 = 2890.25 (−31); Feb 0 1819 = 2952.25 (+31); Mar 0 = 2980.25 (+28), with an alternative 2981.25 for a 29-day February.
- Apr 0 = 3012.25, May 0 = 3042.25, Jun 0 = 3073.25, Nov 0 = 3226.25. This run continues from the leap-year value 2981.25.
- 1818 entries: Jul 0 = 2737.25, Aug 0 = 2768.25, Sep 0 = 2799.25, Oct 0 = 2829.25, Nov 0 = 2860.25, and so on, with differences 31, 31, 30, 31, 30.
The stray string '6.3.12.5.1.2,2' is unexplained.

Overall purpose: to set up Göttingen reduction tables (aberration plus a nutation argument) for 1818–1819 star reductions.
errors: Column (2): log 198.72 = 2.29824, not 2.29894. The written log corresponds to 199.04, so either the coefficient or the log is slipped (or the coefficient is misread).
0 April 1819 = 3012.25024 follows from the leap-year March value 2981.25. With 1819's 28-day February (Mar 0 = 2980.25) it should be 3011.25024; May, June and November 1819 inherit the +1.

Small inconsistency with the previous page. Here the annual node motion is 190.11586337″ × 366.2422 = 69628.45″ = 19°20′28.45″; the previous page has 19°20′28.641″ per solar year. Likewise 18.61303029 years × 366.2422 = 6816.877 sidereal days, versus 6816.89564 here.
μ ≈ 20.61″ (log 1.31408) is larger than the values usual c.1818 (about 20.25″ from Delambre, 20.45″ Lindenau). It is internally consistent with the sinε and cosε logs, though.

results.what: Annual aberration in RA and Dec written linearly in star-independent coefficients a = −μ sinε cosΘ, b = −μ cosε cosΘ, c = −μ sinΘ, with a = b tanε, plus the auxiliary-angle form M sin(ψ+α).

results.modern_name: Mean longitude of the lunar ascending node (nutation argument)

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine practical astronomy: aberration coefficients and a nutation-argument setup for Göttingen reductions around 1819. The day-number-like organisation predates Bessel's 1830 tables, but such linear forms were common, and Gauss is known to have worked on aberration and nutation tables.
